records.name_note: All admissible sources consulted (NC State Extension Plant Toolbox, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder, RHS, UF/IFAS Ask IFAS, UGA CAES Field Report, Clemson HGIC) use the binomial Ilex opaca for American Holly with no synonym or accepted-name conflict among them, so scientific_name_accepted is set to the same binomial as given.
records.toxicity_detail: Fruit is the part described as harmful and not to be eaten. RHS's pet-specific caution states "Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten." NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox separately tags Ilex opaca "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" in its structured Problems list for this species.
unknowns: day_f_max/day_f_min/night_f_max/night_f_min: no admissible source gives specific day/night temperature ranges for this species, only cold-hardiness zone/rating data.

chill_damage_f: only survival-cold data exists (NC State USDA zones 5a-9b, UF/IFAS zones 5B-9, RHS Hardiness H6 = hardy to -20 to -15C); no source gives an actionable damage-onset temperature, so left null as expected for a hardy tree per field guidance.

soil_ph_min: no admissible source states an explicit numeric lower pH bound; UF/IFAS gives only an upper bound ('below 6.5 pH'), and NC State/RHS give only categorical buckets (Acid/Neutral) without a specific floor number.

water_regime and related water_* fields: sources consistently describe a 'moist but well-drained' soil preference (MOBOT, UF/IFAS, RHS, Penn State) alongside separately noted 'high' drought tolerance once established (UF/IFAS, NC State); this combination doesn't map cleanly onto one discrete watering-regime enum value without guessing, so left null as a harm-adjacent field rather than picking a side.
fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: no admissible source addresses a fertilizing schedule, strength, or timing for this species.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives foot-candle figures; NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours...)' is a minimum threshold defining the full-sun category, not a maximum-hours value, so not used for direct_sun_hours_max.
humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source gives numeric ambient humidity percentages; humidity_need was set from Penn State's qualitative 'thrives in humid environments' statement only.

is_houseplant: no admissible source supports growing this species indoors/in containers long-term. UF/IFAS's ST304 lists 'Bonsai' among landscape uses, but for this cold-hardy zone 5-9 tree that denotes outdoor container/bonsai culture, not indoor houseplant growing, so is_houseplant is set false.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox page tags Ilex opaca 'Problem for Cats,' 'Problem for Dogs,' and 'Problem for Horses' as standalone entries in its Problems list, but the page's only detailed poison narrative (Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: 'Nausea, vomiting (not in horses), diarrhea, depression.'; Poison Toxic Principle: 'Illicin, possibly saponic glycosides, and triterpenoids.'; Poison Part: Fruits) is nested under a 'Poisonous to Humans:' sub-header specifically (verified in the page's raw HTML). That symptom/toxic-principle text was NOT used for pet-facing toxicity_detail for this reason; toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail instead rely only on NC State's standalone pet-target tags plus RHS's explicit 'Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten' caution, both of which agree the fruit is the concern.

UF/IFAS ST304 contains two internal inconsistencies between its compact structured fields and its descriptive prose: the structured 'Light requirement' field says 'full sun to full shade' while the prose culture paragraph says 'full sun to partial shade'; the structured 'Soil tolerances' field lists 'acidic; slightly alkaline' while the prose states soils 'below 6.5 pH.' Treated the compact structured tags as likely templated/boilerplate (this ST-series tree fact-sheet format is reused across many species) and used only the specific prose statements for outdoor_sun_exposure and soil_ph_max, consistent with the other five corroborating sources (NC State, MOBOT, RHS, UGA) that all say full sun to part shade rather than full shade.

soil_base: no admissible source uses container/potting-mix terminology for this species; garden_bed was selected as the closest enum fit because every admissible source describes Ilex opaca solely as an in-ground landscape/hedge tree reaching 15 to 60+ feet.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Value is 'moderate' but every citation actually offered for this field says the opposite emphasis: MOBOT (verified quote) says 'well-drained soils... will not tolerate flooding or soils saturated with moisture. Avoid poorly drained soils'; UF/IFAS says 'well-drained but moist'; RHS (re-fetched live and confirmed verbatim) says 'moist but well-drained... Not suited to chalky soils.' No quote in the record, and no live page text, uses 'moderate' or supports a mid-tier/poor-drainage-tolerant reading -- if anything the sources explicitly warn against poor drainage. The value contradicts its own citations.

soil_base — removed on audit: The sole citation quote is 'Design Feature: Barrier Hedge Screen/Privacy Specimen' -- a landscape-use tag describing how the plant is used in design, not a statement about soil or growing medium. It does not say or imply in-ground vs. container growing. The record's own unknowns section admits garden_bed was chosen as 'the closest enum fit' by inference rather than by direct source support, failing the 'does the quote actually state this value' test.

humidity_need — removed on audit: Sole support is one qualitative sentence from an informal Penn State Extension blog post ('Holly Jolly American Holly'), re-fetched and confirmed verbatim: 'It thrives in humid environments with good drainage and moist, slightly acidic soil, yet tolerates a wide range of conditions.' The clause 'yet tolerates a wide range of conditions' undercuts a firm 'high' requirement, no other admissible source corroborates any humidity signal, and the underlying text reads as general native-habitat description rather than an actionable cultivation requirement -- weak grounds for asserting 'high', especially since is_houseplant=false makes an ambient-humidity field questionable for an outdoor tree in the first place.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: Populated as 'Ilex opaca' with a name_note claiming all admissible sources were checked and agree with no synonym conflict, but none of the 9 logged citations contains any quote about nomenclature, synonymy, or an 'accepted name' determination -- the claim isn't traceable to any citation entry as structural check 1/4 require. The value is very likely correct botanically, but as documented in this record it is asserted, not evidenced.

RHS separately gives Prunus persica a Name Status of "Correct" and lists the synonym Amygdalus persica (a slightly different genus-spelling/gender of the same historical name NC State records as Amygdalis persicus). unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max/humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max/light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: these read as indoor-microclimate and container-culture fields; no admissible source discusses ambient indoor temperature, humidity, or foot-candle/sun-hour ceilings for this outdoor orchard/landscape tree.

chill_damage_f: left null despite finding a detailed Penn State Extension frost-critical-temperature table for peach, because the data is genuinely stage-dependent rather than a single damage-onset figure -- 10%-kill temperatures range from 18°F at 'first swelling' up to 28°F at 'post bloom' (with 90%-kill temperatures ranging 1°F to 25°F across the same stages). Picking any single one of these seven values to represent 'the' damage-onset temperature would misrepresent a curve as a point, so the field is left null and the full table is preserved in citations instead.

cool_rest_note: left null. Peach has a real winter-chilling dormancy requirement, but no admissible source gives a single species-wide chill-hour figure -- UGA CAES describes the requirement only in relative terms across cultivars ('less than 600 hours to over 900 hours'), and UF/IFAS frames its numbers explicitly as cultivar- and Florida-region-specific (100 to 650+ chill units, with south-central Florida cultivars needing as few as 75-150 units versus 350-550 for north Florida). Presenting any one of these as the species' cool-rest requirement would misrepresent a range that exists specifically because of intentional low-chill cultivar breeding, so this was left null rather than picking one cultivar group's figure.

water_regime/water_dry_down_target/water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est: left null. This is a harm-capable field and UF/IFAS's own irrigation guidance is stage-dependent in a way that would conflict if forced into one regime: soil water depletion 'should not exceed 25%' during flowering and fruit growth (i.e. keep fairly moist) but 'up to 50%' is allowable during vegetative growth and 'more than 50%... is acceptable' during dormancy (i.e. let it dry out substantially). RHS's potted-peach guidance ('aiming to keep the compost evenly moist') is container-specific and not comparable to in-ground orchard culture. Rather than pick one point on this seasonal curve and label it the species' regime, both the enum field and its numeric companions are left null, with the qualitative detail preserved in water_estimate_basis. UF/IFAS's soil-moisture-sensor check depths (4 and 8 inches, with deeper sensors to 60 inches) are commercial-orchard irrigation-monitoring infrastructure, not a home-gardener 'check by feel' depth, so they were not used to populate water_check_depth_cm either.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: left null. UGA CAES gives a granular-fertilizer schedule by calendar month and tree age (pounds of 10-10-10 and calcium nitrate), not a day-interval figure or a liquid-dilution 'strength' (full/half/quarter) framing, so neither field maps cleanly to what the source actually states.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: populated from UGA CAES's specific numeric range (6-6.5), corroborated qualitatively by Clemson ('near 6.5'). NC State's own soil pH tags for this species ('Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)') and RHS's field ('Acid or Alkaline or Neutral') are broad site-wide categorical buckets rather than a species-curated number, so they were not merged into the numeric field, consistent with how this catalog has treated similar broad-tag-vs-specific-figure situations elsewhere (e.g. Apple, Red Maple).

is_houseplant: left false. RHS documents that 'compact varieties can also be grown in containers' and 'can also be grown in an unheated greenhouse for all or part of the year,' with potted trees only moved to 'a greenhouse, porch or other frost-free spot during flowering' for frost protection -- this is outdoor/greenhouse container culture for fruit production, not indoor long-term houseplant use, so is_houseplant was kept false rather than set true on the container-growing evidence, consistent with how this catalog has treated similar outdoor-container language for other landscape/orchard trees (e.g. Crape Myrtle).

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: toxic_to_pets true is supported directly by NC State's own '#problem for dogs' and '#problem for cats' tags (a structured field distinct from, not blended with, the page's human-specific 'Poisonous to Humans' poison-severity block). NC State also tags '#problem for horses,' but per this catalog's established convention horses are not treated as within the 'toxic_to_pets' boolean's scope (they are, however, preserved in toxicity_detail via Penn State's peach-naming corroboration). No admissible source gives dog/cat-specific symptoms or a dog/cat-specific toxic dose for this species beyond the tag itself, so toxicity_detail describes the human-targeted poison data and the general wilted-leaf/seed hazard separately from the bare pet tags, rather than presenting the human symptom list as if it had been established for pets.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Two separate traceability failures. (1) The citation labeled 'toxicity_detail poison part Seeds, toxic principle cyanogenic glycoside/amygdalin, severity Medium (Poisonous to Humans section)' asserts 'severity Medium' in its claim, but its own quote text -- 'Poison Symptoms: Gasping, weakness, excitement, pupil dilation, spasms, convulsions, coma, respiratory failure. Poison Toxic Principle: Cyanogenic glycoside, amygdalin. Poison Part: Seeds' -- contains no severity rating at all, so 'Medium' (which the toxicity_detail field text repeats verbatim) doesn't trace to any quote. (2) The toxicity_detail field text includes a direct quotation -- "highest in both new growth and wilted leaves and branches" -- attributed to the Penn State horse-pasture source, but no citation entry in the array contains this string; the only Penn State citation quotes just 'Apricot and peach trees are in the same genus (Prunus) and are thought to contain the same toxins in the leaves and seeds.' The field's own text further admits the wilted-leaf/new-growth detail describes 'related Prunus species,' not peach itself -- exactly the sibling-species-boilerplate problem the audit brief flags. On top of this, the field centers a full human-poisoning symptom list (gasping, pupil dilation, coma) inside what is supposed to be pet-toxicity detail, sourced explicitly from NC State's human-only 'Poisonous to Humans' section, with no animal-specific symptom data anywhere in the citations.

water_estimate_basis — removed on audit: The field presents 'up to 50%... is allowable' (vegetative growth) and 'more than 50%... is acceptable' (dormancy) as quoted soil-water-depletion targets from UF/IFAS HS1316, but the only citation supporting this claim quotes solely 'soil water depletion should not exceed 25% of the available soil water.' No citation in the array contains the 50% figures for either growth stage, so two of the three stage-specific numbers in this field are untraceable to any source quote and should be treated as unverified. This also undermines the stated rationale for leaving water_regime null, since that rationale leans on the same unsupported 50% figures to argue the guidance is stage-dependent.

fertilize_active_months — removed on audit: The sole supporting citation's quote is explicitly scoped to first-year trees: 'Do not fertilize newly planted, first year, peach trees until March... In May, broadcast... In July, broadcast...' The field generalizes this first-year-only fertilizer regimen into a blanket species-wide fertilize_active_months value with no age qualification, which would misapply a young-tree schedule to mature/bearing peach trees (extension sources typically differentiate fertilizer timing and amount by tree age).

soil_base — removed on audit: The citation backing 'garden_bed' quotes only 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage / Moist' from NC State's structured data tags -- a drainage-rate characteristic, not any statement about whether the tree is grown in-ground, in a raised bed, or in a container. Nothing in that quote supports the claim label's parenthetical '(in-ground landscape/orchard tree).' No other citation in the array cleanly establishes in-ground growing as the primary substrate either -- one RHS citation used elsewhere in the record for is_houseplant even notes 'compact varieties can also be grown in containers,' which cuts against treating garden_bed as the uncontested default.

records.name_note: All admissible sources consulted (NC State Extension, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, UF/IFAS, Penn State Extension, UGA Extension) consistently use Pyrus communis as the current binomial for the common/European pear; no conflicting accepted name was found.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: left null. UF/IFAS states open blossoms are usually killed at 26°F or below; Penn State Extension states flowers can be killed and fruit set severely reduced below 28°F. These are two different damage-onset thresholds from admissible sources with no resolving source, so the field is left null per the harm-capable-field conflict rule rather than picking one.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: left null. No admissible source (NC State, MOBOT, RHS, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UGA, Clemson) addresses toxicity of Pyrus communis to pets or humans; not inferred from the Rosaceae family.

soil_ph: NC State's Plant Toolbox lists a standardized site-wide category 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' for this field, which reads as a generic pH bucket applied broadly across their database rather than pear-specific research. The record instead uses UGA Extension's specific researched figure ('pH of 5.9 to 6.5') as the more reliable species-specific value; RHS's prose ('fairly neutral soil... will not thrive on very acid soils') is broadly consistent with both.
direct_sun_hours_max: left null. NC State gives only a full-sun minimum ('6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day'); no admissible source states an upper bound on sun hours.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good: left null. No admissible source quantifies humidity or light level (foot-candles) for this outdoor landscape/orchard tree.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, cool_rest_note: left null. These read as houseplant comfort-range/dormancy fields; admissible sources instead describe Pyrus communis's cold tolerance only as USDA zones 4-8 (MOBOT, NC State) and as a blossom/frost-damage threshold (captured, in conflict, under chill_damage_f), not as day/night temperature preferences.

water_regime, water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: left null. No admissible source frames watering for this in-ground orchard tree as a dry-down/moisture-check cycle. UF/IFAS gives Florida-specific sandy-soil irrigation amounts (mature trees 50+ gallons, young trees 2-3 gallons per application, every 7-10 days in dry seasons) but this is regional guidance tied to Florida soils/climate, not a general species watering regime, so it was not forced into these fields.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: left null. Sources describe fertilizing as a twice-yearly split application tied either to growth stage (UGA: before growth begins / after fruit set) or to fixed months in Florida's climate (UF/IFAS: January and June, used for fertilize_active_months), not as a fixed day-interval or a diluted 'strength'.

UF/IFAS HS1393 ('The Pear (Pyrus spp.) in Florida Home Gardens') covers pear culture in Florida generally, spanning both Pyrus communis (European pear) and Asian pear types; its fertilizer-month recommendation was used for this record because the document explicitly names P. communis as one of the two pear groups in scope and gives no differing guidance by type, but it is Florida-climate-specific and may not generalize to all growing regions.

UF/IFAS 'Pyrus communis, Common Pear' (FOR293/FR361), a Florida forestry fact sheet found via search, returned HTTP 410 Gone on ask.ifas.ufl.edu at the time of research and could not be fetched or used as a citation despite being referenced in search-result summaries.

fertilize_active_months — removed on audit: I fetched the UF/IFAS HS1393 source directly. Its Fertilization section opens with: 'UF/IFAS has not researched fertilizer requirements for pear. Therefore, we suggest a general fertilizer like 6-6-6 or 8-8-8.' The January/June split-application timing used for this field is that same unresearched, generic suggestion — not species- or even genus-researched guidance — and the document explicitly covers both European and Asian pear without distinguishing the schedule by type. It is also Florida-climate-specific (assumes no hard winter dormancy in January), which is the identical defect the record itself correctly used to exclude this same document's irrigation-gallon figures from water_regime ('this is regional guidance tied to Florida soils/climate, not a general species watering regime, so it was not forced into these fields'). Applying stricter regional-specificity scrutiny to water than to fertilizer timing from the identical source is an internal inconsistency, and for pear's actual USDA zone 4-8 range (per MOBOT/NC State), a January fertilizer application would be inappropriate in most of that range.

scientific_name_accepted: restored using NC State's taxonomy block (Genus/Species/Family), which the audit itself located and confirmed on the live page -- the original citation quoted a descriptive sentence instead of this block, which is what actually states the binomial.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: NC State's 'Problem for Dogs' tag has no supporting mechanism in any admissible source checked (Clemson, MOBOT, RHS, Penn State, UMD, UGA); it is included in toxic_to_pets=true on the strength of NC State's own structured Problems field, matching this catalog's established precedent (e.g. Ficus carica) that an unexplained 'Problem for [animal]' structured tag is sufficient support for toxic_to_pets even without a separate prose detail, as long as it isn't a human-only heading being misapplied. The horse hazard, by contrast, does have a specific documented mechanism (Penn State: bedding-shavings-induced laminitis; leaf/pollen respiratory signs).

Juglone/allelopathy (toxicity to OTHER PLANTS, not pets): every admissible source addressing this (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, Penn State x2, UMD, UGA x2) describes it as harming nearby plants -- azaleas, peonies, tomatoes, apples, blueberries, rhododendrons, solanaceous crops -- via root/leaf/hull exudate. This is deliberately NOT folded into toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail, which is scoped to animal harm; there is no dedicated allelopathy field in this schema, so the plant-hazard information itself has no field to populate. Two nuances worth flagging: UGA's 'Did You Know You Can Grow: Black Walnut' article makes one broader, unelaborated claim that 'Juglone can harm animals and humans' (used only as light corroboration for toxic_to_pets, not as a standalone basis); and UMD Extension separately notes the juglone-causes-poor-plant-growth link itself is scientifically disputed ('there is no conclusive, science-based evidence confirming juglone as the cause...'), a caveat about the allelopathy claim's strength that doesn't affect any field in this record.

Clemson Cooperative Extension (hgic.clemson.edu) has no dedicated Juglans nigra/black walnut fact sheet -- confirmed via site search and its Nuts category listing, which covers only pecan and general chill-hours content -- so Clemson could not be used as a citation source for this record. UF/IFAS's only black walnut publication (EDIS/Ask IFAS ENH479/ST320) returned HTTP 410 Gone on direct fetch as of this research (the URL redirects to an Ask IFAS 'no longer available' page) and likewise could not be used.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Two defects. (1) Citation-traceability gap: the clause 'not for cats -- a separate site tag reads "non-toxic for cats"' has zero supporting citation entry. I fetched the live NC State page and confirmed the '#non-toxic for cats' tag is real, but it lives in the page's general tag cloud, not in the structured 'Problems:' dt/dd list, and the only toxic_to_pets citation in the record quotes just 'Problems: Allelopathic / Problem for Dogs / Problem for Horses.' A true fact stated with no citation backing it still fails the 'every non-null field value traces to a citation entry' rule. (2) Mislabeled/blended citation: the UGA quote used as animal corroboration -- 'Juglone is a strong respiratory toxin and small amounts will damage other living creatures' -- is presented in the citation label as 'juglone is a respiratory toxin to other creatures' (i.e. animal-toxicity support). I fetched the full source article (fieldreport.caes.uga.edu/news/your-black-walnut-tree-is-out-to-get-you/) and found that sentence is immediately followed, in the same paragraph, by 'In the soil, juglone will damage many living things, including plant roots' -- it is the transition sentence into the article's plant-root/soil-allelopathy section, not a standalone animal-toxicity statement. In juglone allelopathy literature, 'respiratory toxin' is the standard term for juglone inhibiting cellular respiration in plant root cells (the core allelopathy mechanism), not an animal inhalation hazard -- Penn State's own horse-specific mechanism is bedding-contact laminitis and possible pollen/leaf respiratory irritation, never described this way. The citation's quote is truncated with an ellipsis exactly before the plant-transition sentence, making an allelopathy-context line read as clean animal corroboration. This is the specific plant-hazard-blended-into-toxicity_detail failure mode the audit brief asked to check for.

records.name_note: Admissible sources give genuinely conflicting resolutions of the accepted name, so scientific_name_accepted is left null. NC State Extension's own dedicated species page uses "Sambucus canadensis" as the current name and explicitly lists "Sambucus nigra subsp. canadensis" under a "Previously known as" heading -- i.e., NC State treats the subspecies-of-nigra treatment as superseded. The Royal Horticultural Society resolves the identical pair in the opposite direction: its page for "Sambucus nigra subsp. canadensis" carries "Name Status: Correct" together with "Synonym: Sambucus canadensis," while its separate page for the plain binomial "Sambucus canadensis" is itself marked "Name Status: Synonym." UF/IFAS's EDIS/Ask IFAS publications (ENH-736/ST578 and FE1093) use "Sambucus nigra ssp. canadensis" as their working scientific name throughout ("Scientific name: Sambucus nigra ssp. canadensis"). Missouri Botanical Garden files its profile under "Sambucus canadensis" but flags the same unresolved split in its own text: "Some authorities consider this plant to be a subspecies or variety of Sambucus nigra instead of a separate species." Because NC State and RHS actively resolve this in opposite directions, and MOBOT and UF/IFAS split the same way without resolving it themselves, no single accepted binomial is asserted here.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The value is serialized as the JSON string "null" (with quotes) rather than an actual null. Every other unresolved field in the record (toxic_to_pets, chill_damage_f, water_regime, etc.) uses a bare null. A string "null" is truthy/non-empty to virtually any downstream consumer, so this field would render as populated with garbage text instead of correctly signaling 'unknown/unresolved' -- silently defeating the careful genuine-conflict reasoning documented in name_note. normalizations: 2026-08-23: tenth batch of the "blind spots" pass. American Holly confirmed toxic_to_pets=true (a classic holiday plant with well-documented berry toxicity, extremely common as a landscape hedge). Rounded out with more fruit/nut trees (Peach, Pear, Pecan), Black Walnut (with its two distinct, easy-to-conflate hazards -- juglone allelopathy toxic to other plants, versus bedding-contact laminitis in horses), American Elderberry (edible-cooked/toxic-raw pattern), and two ornamental categories new to this catalog: Fountain Grass and Pachysandra groundcover.

Two landing-time repairs, both restoring already-available evidence the audit itself located: Pear's scientific_name_accepted was nulled because the record quoted a descriptive sentence instead of NC State's taxonomy block, which the audit fetched directly and confirmed reads "Genus: Pyrus Species: communis Family: Rosaceae" -- added as a proper citation and restored. Fountain Grass's common_name was nulled after the audit caught an undisclosed cherry-pick: 3 of the 5 sources actually cited (RHS, NC State, UMD) call it "Chinese Fountain Grass" specifically, already quoted in the record's own citations, while the record silently used the minority plain form -- restored to the majority, already-cited name.

Black Walnut's toxicity_detail catch is a precise example of the plant-hazard-vs-animal-hazard confusion this batch's species note specifically warned about: a UGA quote calling juglone "a strong respiratory toxin" was being used as animal-toxicity evidence, but the audit traced the full source paragraph and found that sentence is the transition into the article's plant-root/soil allelopathy section (the standard meaning of "respiratory toxin" in juglone literature is inhibiting cellular respiration in root cells, not an animal inhalation hazard) -- correctly excluded rather than presented as pet-relevant.

Fountain Grass surfaced a genuine taxonomic split this catalog hasn't hit before with an even split rather than a majority: RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden both anchor to Pennisetum alopecuroides as accepted, while NC State Extension and University of Maryland Extension both independently anchor to Cenchrus alopecuroides -- landed with scientific_name_accepted null and the full four-source conflict documented in name_note.

Pennisetum's own scientific_name_accepted also carried the same string-"null"-instead-of-JSON-null bug seen in b23/b24/b27, again caught and self-corrected by the auditor's own explicit finding before this landing pass even ran its check.
